sec.h: Fields of glass in the desert

sec.t:
Not all solar power comes from giant parks. In 2024 the government started a scheme called PM Surya Ghar, which helps families pay for rooftop panels. A home can use the electricity it makes, and in many states it can sell extra power back to the grid. By August 2026, rooftop panels across India added up to about 33 GW.

Farmers are using solar pumps to water fields instead of diesel pumps. Some villages far from power lines run on small solar grids of their own. [[@india-wonder-sun-temple-modhera|Modhera]] in Gujarat was declared India's first round-the-clock solar-powered village in 2022, using rooftop panels and a big battery.

A solar panel is a sandwich of thin slices of silicon, the same material used in computer chips. When sunlight strikes the silicon, it knocks tiny charged particles called [[electron|electrons]] loose, and wires collect them as an electric current. This is called the [[photovoltaic|photovoltaic]] effect, from the Greek word for light and the name of the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta.

For years, most panels and cells used in India were made in China. The government now offers money and rules that favour Indian-made panels, and new factories have opened in Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and other states. Making more of the parts at home is meant to create jobs and protect India from shortages.

The Sun sets every evening, and clouds roll in during the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. Solar panels can't help when people switch on lights and fans at night. So India is building giant [[@batteries-future|batteries]] to store daytime power, and pairing solar with wind farms, which often blow hardest in the evening and in the rainy season.

Land is another puzzle. Solar parks need a lot of space, and India has many people and farms. One answer is floating solar, with panels placed on [[reservoir|reservoirs]] and lakes. A large floating project has been set up, in stages, on the Omkareshwar reservoir on the [[@narmada|Narmada river]] in Madhya Pradesh.

In 2015, at the [[climate|climate]] talks in Paris, India and France launched the International Solar Alliance, a group of countries working together to spread solar power. Its headquarters are in Gurugram, near Delhi. More than 100 countries have signed up, many of them sunny nations in Africa, Asia and South America.

Solar power is one of the cheapest ways to make electricity today. Each panel that replaces coal means less smoke in the air and less of the gas that drives [[@climate-change|climate change]].

text: The Kushans were a ruling family descended from the Yuezhi, a nomadic people who herded horses in north-western China. Pushed west by enemies in the 2nd century BCE, the Yuezhi settled in Bactria, in today's northern Afghanistan. One of their clans, the Kushans, united the others.

By the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, Kushan kings ruled a huge stretch of land from Central Asia across Afghanistan and Pakistan to Mathura and beyond on the Ganga plains. They grew rich by sitting astride the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]], the web of routes linking China, India, Persia and Rome. Their greatest king, Kanishka, is remembered as a patron of Buddhism and art.

st.prompt: Kanishka's gold coins show gods from many religions. Which mix appears on them?

options.t: Greek, Iranian and Indian gods, and the Buddha
Only Hindu gods
Only the king himself, with no gods at all

st.reveal: Kushan coins carry a crowd of gods, including the Greek sun god Helios, Iranian gods of fire and wind, the Indian god Shiva and the Buddha. The kings ruled people of many faiths and seem to have wanted all of them on side.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kushan dynasty.
British Museum, Kushan coins and the Bimaran casket.
n.certNote: Historians agree on who the Kushans were and roughly where they ruled. The dates of their greatest king, Kanishka, are still argued over; many scholars now favour a start around 127 CE, while older books link him to 78 CE.

sec.h: From the steppe to the Hindu Kush
sec.t:
Chinese historians tell the early story. The Yuezhi lost a war with the Xiongnu, another nomadic people, and moved thousands of kilometres west with their herds. A Chinese envoy named Zhang Qian visited them in Bactria around 128 BCE, hoping to make an alliance. They politely refused. They had settled down and liked their new home.

In the 1st century CE, a chief called Kujula Kadphises joined the five Yuezhi clans into one kingdom. His successors pushed south over the Hindu Kush into the plains of the Indus and the Ganga.

Kushan coins are one of the best sources about them. The kings issued plentiful gold coins, perhaps using gold that came in through trade with Rome. The coins use Greek letters to write Bactrian, an Iranian language, and some carry [[@scripts-india|Indian scripts]] too.

On the back, they show a crowd of gods: Greek, Iranian and Indian. A coin of Kanishka shows a standing figure labelled BODDO, the Buddha. It was a clever message from rulers of many peoples. Merchants from Rome to China would handle these coins and see a powerful, welcoming [[empire|empire]].

Under the Kushans, two great schools of [[@sculpture|sculpture]] grew up. In Gandhara, around Peshawar and Taxila, artists carved the [[@buddha|Buddha]] in grey stone with wavy hair and heavy robes in folds, showing the influence of Greek styles that had lingered since [[@alexander-india|Alexander]]. At Mathura, artists worked in spotted red sandstone and gave the Buddha a rounder, more Indian look.

Until about this time, artists had shown the Buddha only through symbols. Kushan-era sculptors made the human image of the Buddha common. Their ideas travelled along the Silk Road to Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan.

In the 3rd century CE, the new Sasanian rulers of Persia took the western Kushan lands. Smaller Kushan kings held on in the Punjab for a while, but the empire broke apart. In northern India, the Guptas later rose in the space they left. The Kushans' stone Buddhas, scattered across museums from Mathura to Kabul to London, are the clearest trace of the riders who once crossed half of Asia.

text: In 1587, about 115 English settlers arrived on Roanoke Island, off the coast of what is now North Carolina, USA. Their governor, John White, sailed back to England for supplies. War with Spain delayed his return for three years.

When he finally came back in August 1590, the settlement was empty. The houses had been taken down. Carved into a post was the word CROATOAN, and the letters CRO were cut into a tree. There was no sign of a struggle and no bodies. White was never able to search further, and the colonists were never seen by English eyes again.

st.prompt: Before leaving, John White agreed on a secret signal with the colonists. What did it mean if they carved a cross above a place name?

options.t: They had left in danger
They had found gold
They had gone back to England

st.reveal: If they moved, they were to carve where they went. A cross meant they had been forced out or were in trouble. White found the word CROATOAN with no cross, which gave him hope.

src: U.S. National Park Service, Fort Raleigh National Historic Site.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, Lost Colony.
n.certNote: Nobody knows what happened to the colonists. Historians and archaeologists favour different explanations, and new finds keep the debate going.

d.try: With a friend, agree on a secret sign that means "I'm fine" and another that means "help". Then write a short message using only one word and a sign. Swap and see what the other person thinks happened. It shows how much meaning, and how much confusion, one word can carry.
myth: The Roanoke colonists vanished without a single clue.
They left a clear clue, the word CROATOAN, the name of a nearby island and the Native people who lived there. The mystery is what happened after that, not whether they left a message.
facts: John White, an artist and mapmaker

sec.t:
This was one of England's earliest attempts to settle in North America, more than 30 years before the *Mayflower*. An earlier group had tried in 1585 but gave up and sailed home the next year.

The 1587 colonists included families, not just soldiers. Among them was White's daughter, Eleanor Dare. On 18 August 1587, she gave birth to a girl named Virginia, the first child born to English parents in the Americas.

The settlers relied on trade and help from local Native nations. Relations with some were friendly, and with others tense. A man named Manteo, from the Croatoan people, had travelled to England and back and acted as a guide and translator.

sec.h: Idea one: they joined the Croatoan
sec.t:
Croatoan was the name of an island about 80 km south, now part of Hatteras Island, and of the people who lived there. Manteo came from there. Many historians think the colonists, short of food, went to live with the Croatoan and slowly became part of their community.

[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] digging on Hatteras since the late 1990s have found English objects from the right period, such as a piece of a sword handle, a slate for writing and bits of metal. But such items could also have come through trade, so the finds don't settle the case.

In 2012, researchers at the British Museum studied John White's own map of the region. Under a patch of paper, they spotted a hidden symbol that looked like a fort, about 80 km inland near the Albemarle Sound.

Was it a planned new home? A team began digging near the spot and found English pottery that might belong to the colonists. Others think the pieces come from later settlers. [[@maps-history|Old maps]] can hold secrets, but they don't always explain them.

Some colonists may have died from disease, hunger or conflict. The years around 1587 had severe [[drought|droughts]], shown by tree rings from very old cypress trees in the area. A failed harvest would have been hard on everyone, settlers and Native people alike.

It's also possible the group split up, with some going south and some inland. That would explain why both theories turn up evidence.

The lost colony has become a legend in America, and every summer a play about it is performed on Roanoke Island. It also reminds us that the land was already home to many [[@native-nations|Native nations]], whose own histories of this time were rarely written down by Europeans.

Archaeologists keep digging, using careful methods described in [[@archaeology|how archaeology works]]. One new find could change the answer. Until then, a single carved word is the last message from 115 people.

text: When British rule over India ended in August 1947, the land was split into two countries: India and Pakistan. Pakistan itself came in two pieces, West Pakistan and East Pakistan, about 1,600 km apart with India in between.

The split, called Partition, divided the provinces of [[@punjab|Punjab]] and Bengal roughly along religious lines. Areas with Muslim majorities went to Pakistan and the rest stayed with India. Millions of Hindus and Sikhs moved one way and millions of Muslims the other. It was one of the largest movements of people in history, and the violence that came with it killed hundreds of thousands, possibly far more.

st.reveal: The Radcliffe Line was kept secret until 17 August, partly so it would not spoil the independence celebrations. Millions of people in Punjab and Bengal celebrated freedom without knowing which country their village was in.

n.certNote: Nobody counted the dead or the displaced properly at the time. Estimates of deaths range from about 2 lakh to 20 lakh, and of people forced to move from about 1 crore to 2 crore. Historians also disagree about who was most responsible.

d.try: Many families in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh have stories from 1947. If someone in your family or neighbourhood is happy to talk about it, ask an older person what they remember hearing. Write down their story in their own words and keep it, because these memories are disappearing.
myth: Partition happened only along India's western border with Pakistan.
Bengal in the east was split too. East Bengal became East Pakistan, and in 1971 it became the independent country of Bangladesh.

sec.t:
By the 1940s, Britain was weakened by the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] and ready to leave India. The question was what would replace British rule.

The Indian National Congress, led by people like [[@nehru|Nehru]] and [[@gandhi|Gandhi]], wanted one united India. The Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, argued that Muslims would be outnumbered in a Hindu-majority country and needed a homeland of their own. In 1940 the League formally demanded what became Pakistan.

Talks failed, and trust between the groups broke down. In 1946 riots broke out in Calcutta and spread. Historians still argue over how much blame belongs to British policy, to the League, or to Congress. Most agree all three made choices that led there.

sec.h: A line drawn in a hurry
sec.t:
In early 1947, Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy, brought the date of British withdrawal forward by almost a year, to August 1947. That left very little time.

Sir Cyril Radcliffe was given about five weeks to draw borders through Punjab and Bengal. He had never visited India, worked from old maps and [[@census|census]] figures, and hardly left his office in Delhi. The line he drew cut through farms, rivers, railway lines and even villages. Lahore went to Pakistan, Amritsar to India.

As the border became known, fear spread. People who suddenly found themselves a minority packed what they could carry and left homes their families had lived in for generations. They walked in columns many kilometres long, rode bullock carts, or crammed into and on top of trains.

{{story:refugees}}

There were terrible attacks on all sides, especially in Punjab. Many women and children suffered. At the same time, there are many stories of neighbours who hid and protected each other at great risk.

In Bengal, Gandhi went on a fast in Calcutta in September 1947, refusing food until the fighting stopped. Leaders from different communities promised peace, and the city calmed.

The new countries had to look after crores of [[@refugees|refugees]]. Camps grew around Delhi and other cities. Whole new neighbourhoods and towns appeared, such as Faridabad near Delhi, built partly for families from the west.

Partition also left a dispute over [[@kashmir|Kashmir]] that India and Pakistan still argue about. In 1971, East Pakistan broke away to become [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]].

For many years families talked about 1947 only quietly. Writers such as Saadat Hasan Manto and Khushwant Singh wrote stories about it. In 2017 the Partition Museum opened in Amritsar's old Town Hall, collecting objects people carried with them: keys to houses they never saw again, letters, and a few cooking pots.

Today the [[@border-crossings|border at Wagah]], between Amritsar and Lahore, holds a flag ceremony every evening, with soldiers of both countries marching on either side of the line.

text: The Vikings were seafaring people from Scandinavia, today's [[@norway-fjords|Norway]], Denmark and Sweden, who sailed out between roughly 793 and 1066 CE. Some raided [[monastery|monasteries]] and towns. Many more traded, farmed and settled new lands.

In their fast longships they reached Britain, Ireland and France, sailed rivers deep into [[@russia|Russia]] and Ukraine, and traded as far as Constantinople and Baghdad. They settled [[@iceland|Iceland]] and [[@world-greenland|Greenland]], and around 1000 CE they reached North America. The word "Viking" probably meant someone who went on sea raids. Most Scandinavians of the time were farmers, and only some went "a-viking".

sec.h: The raid that started it all
sec.t:
In 793, raiders landed at Lindisfarne, a monastery on an island off northeast England. They took treasures and killed or captured monks. An English scholar wrote that nobody had thought such a voyage possible.

For the next two centuries, Viking fleets raided coasts and rivers across Europe. They sacked [[@paris|Paris]] in 845. Later, many settled where they had raided. A Viking leader named Rollo was given land in northern France around 911, which became Normandy, "the land of the Northmen".

Icelandic sagas tell of Leif Erikson sailing west from Greenland around 1000 CE to a land he called Vinland. For centuries, people wondered if the story was true.

In 1960, explorers Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found the remains of Viking-style buildings at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, [[@canada|Canada]]. In 2021, scientists studied wood cut with metal tools at the site. A burst of [[radiation|radiation]] from the Sun in 993 left a marker in tree rings, letting them count forward to the exact year the trees were cut: 1021. That is 471 years before [[@columbus|Columbus]] crossed the Atlantic.

Vikings traded furs, [[@amber-fossils|amber]], walrus ivory and slaves for silver, silk and spices. Tens of thousands of Arabic silver coins have been found in Scandinavia.

On Helgö, an island in a lake near Stockholm, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] in 1954 dug up a small bronze statue of the [[@buddha|Buddha]], made in northern South Asia around the 6th century. It reached a Swedish trading settlement that later became part of the Viking world, passed along trade routes from hand to hand.

Vikings worshipped gods such as Odin, Thor and Freya. Three English days of the week are named after Norse gods: Wednesday after Woden, or Odin; Thursday after Thor; and Friday after Frigg. English also borrowed Norse words such as sky, egg, knife and window.

They wrote with letters called runes, carved on stones and sticks. In Iceland, Viking settlers founded an assembly called the Althing in 930, which still meets as the country's [[parliament|parliament]]. The Viking Age ended around 1066, as Scandinavian kingdoms became Christian and settled into European ways.

text: A border crossing is an official place where people and goods move from one country to another. Usually there are two kinds of check. Immigration officers check who you are and whether you are allowed in. They look at your passport, and sometimes a visa, which is permission to enter. [[customs|Customs]] officers check what you are carrying, to stop banned goods and to collect tax on certain items.

Crossings can be busy road posts with long queues of lorries, quiet country lanes, [[@airports|airports]], seaports or railway stations. Some borders are so open that you barely notice them. Others are tightly guarded. What happens at a border depends on how the two countries get along and what agreements they have made.

facts: Longest land border between two countries
Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar

sec.h: Who are you, and what are you carrying?

sec.t:
India shares land borders with six countries: Pakistan, China, Nepal, [[@bhutan|Bhutan]], [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]] and Myanmar. With two of them, Nepal and Bhutan, the border is open for each other's citizens.

At the town of Jaigaon in West Bengal, a decorated gate leads straight into Phuentsholing in Bhutan. Indians can walk through with simple ID. On the India–Nepal border, buses and bicycles cross each day, carrying workers, students, shoppers and families visiting relatives.

sec.h: Ceremonies and lines on the floor
sec.t:
At Attari–Wagah, between Amritsar in India and Lahore in Pakistan, soldiers from both sides hold a flag-lowering ceremony at sunset. It features high kicks, stamping and loud cheers from crowds on each side, and it is a big tourist attraction.

The US and Canada share the longest land border between two countries, about 8,900 km. In the towns of Derby Line, in Vermont, and Stanstead, in Quebec, the Haskell Free Library and Opera House was deliberately built across the border in the early 1900s. A black line on the floor marks it, and the stage of its opera house is in Canada while most of the seats are in the US.

Some borders twist in odd ways. In Baarle, a town on the Belgian–Dutch border, little pieces of Belgium sit inside the Netherlands, and pieces of the Netherlands inside those. The line runs through houses, cafés and shops, marked by crosses on the pavement.

India and Bangladesh once had over 160 [[enclave|enclaves]], small pockets of one country surrounded by the other. People living in them often struggled to get schools, hospitals or ID cards. In 2015 the two countries swapped the enclaves, and the residents could choose which country to belong to.

In much of Europe, 29 countries form the Schengen Area. People usually drive or take a train from, say, France to Germany without stopping at all, though checks can be brought back for a time.

Not everyone crosses borders by choice. [[@refugees|Refugees]] flee war or danger and may arrive with few papers. International laws say they should be allowed to ask for protection.

text: The Hornbill Festival is a ten-day celebration held every year from 1 to 10 December in Nagaland, in northeast India. It takes place at the Kisama Heritage Village, about 12 km from the state capital, Kohima, and brings together the many Naga tribes to share their dances, songs, food, crafts and games.

The Nagaland government started it in 2000 to celebrate Naga culture, encourage tribes to meet each other and attract tourists. It has grown into one of India's most famous festivals. In 2025, the 26th edition drew visitors and performers from across India and several other countries.

options.t: A traditional village dormitory where young people learned their community's skills and stories
A kind of drum carved from a tree trunk
A spicy pork curry

st.reveal: In many Naga villages, the morung was a large house where young men, and in some communities young women, lived and learned crafts, songs, history and how to defend the village. At Kisama, each tribe builds its own morung in its own style.

It was started by the Nagaland government in 2000. It brings together the separate traditional festivals of many tribes, which are much older, into one shared celebration.

sec.t:
Kisama Heritage Village is like a living museum. Each major Naga tribe, including the Angami, Ao, Konyak, Lotha, Sumi and others, has built its own morung there. A morung is a traditional house where young people once lived together and learned their community's history, songs and skills.

Walking through Kisama, you can see how the tribes differ. Each has its own style of house, carving, [[weaving|weaving]] and dress. Shawls show patterns that tell which tribe a person belongs to and, in some groups, what honours their family has earned.

The days are packed. Groups in full traditional dress perform dances, many with spears, shields and long rows of dancers singing together. Huge log drums, carved from single tree trunks, boom across the hills.

There are sports too: Naga wrestling, archery and traditional games. Craft markets sell bamboo baskets, beadwork and handwoven shawls. Visitors can try traditional games, watch contests in old skills such as making fire without matches, and taste food cooked in bamboo tubes. At night, the Hornbill International Rock Contest turns Kohima into a music festival, because Nagaland has a strong love of rock music and many young bands.

Naga food is famous for smoked pork, bamboo shoots, fermented soybeans and fiery chillies. One festival event is a chilli-eating contest featuring the Naga king chilli, also called bhut jolokia or ghost pepper.

In 2007, Guinness World Records named the bhut jolokia the world's hottest [[@chillies|chilli]]. It has since been overtaken by peppers bred in the USA, such as the Carolina Reaper and Pepper X. Contestants still need plenty of courage and plenty of rice. Food stalls offer dishes from every tribe, and the festival is a feast of [[@northeast-food|northeast Indian food]].

Nagaland has 16 or more officially recognised tribes and dozens of languages and [[dialect|dialects]]. In the past, many villages were isolated by steep hills and forests. The festival gives tribes a shared stage, while keeping their differences. Many Nagas speak Nagamese, a mixed language, or English to understand each other across tribes.

It also brings money into a region far from big cities. Hotels, homestays and taxi drivers depend on the festival crowds. At the same time, Naga elders and young people use it to pass on songs and skills that might otherwise fade, part of the wider story of India's [[@people-tribes-india|tribal communities]].

text: Kashmir is a high valley in the Himalaya, ringed by snowy mountains, with lakes, rivers, orchards and gardens on its floor. People have called it beautiful for centuries. It is famous for [[@oddity-floating-post-office|Dal Lake]] and its houseboats, for saffron and apples, for soft shawls, and for a grand feast called the wazwan.

The name is also used for a much larger region, and this is where things get complicated. Since 1947, the wider Kashmir region has been divided between India and Pakistan, with a part controlled by China. Each country claims areas held by the others, and the dispute has led to wars and long periods of tension. This article is mostly about the valley on the Indian side, around the city of Srinagar.

st.prompt: In freezing Kashmiri winters, many people keep warm with a "kangri". What is it?

options.t: A small clay pot of hot coals in a wicker basket, held under a long cloak
A heated stone bench by the front door
A thick blanket made from yak hair

st.reveal: A kangri is a clay pot filled with glowing embers, wrapped in woven wicker. People hold it inside their pheran, a long, loose woollen cloak, like a portable heater. It needs care, because the embers are very hot.

myth: Kashmir is cold and snowy all year round.

The valley has four clear seasons. Winters are freezing and snowy, but summers are warm and green, with temperatures often above 30 °C in Srinagar. Spring brings tulips and almond blossom, and autumn turns the chinar trees red.

sec.t:
Dal Lake lies at the edge of Srinagar, with mountains reflected in its water. Hundreds of carved wooden houseboats are moored along its shores. Visitors are rowed around in shikaras, narrow boats with painted roofs and cushioned seats.

Parts of the lake hold floating gardens, made from mats of reeds and weeds piled with soil. Farmers grow tomatoes, lotus stems and greens on them. Early in the morning, a floating vegetable market gathers on the water, with sellers and buyers bargaining from boat to boat.

Each autumn, fields around the town of Pampore bloom with purple saffron crocuses. Each flower has three red threads, the stigmas, picked by hand. It takes around 150 flowers to make one gram of [[@saffron|saffron]], which is why it costs so much.

Kashmir is also known for pashmina, a very fine [[@wool|wool]] combed from the soft undercoat of mountain goats that live high on the cold plateau of Ladakh and Tibet. Kashmiri weavers spin and weave it into shawls so light that, people say, a fine one can be pulled through a finger ring. Craftspeople also make papier-mâché boxes, carpets and walnut-wood carvings.

The coldest stretch of winter is called Chillai Kalan, about 40 days from late December to the end of January. Snow can cut off roads, and parts of Dal Lake sometimes freeze. People wear the pheran, a long woollen cloak, and keep warm with a kangri, a small pot of hot coals held underneath it.

Food helps too. Families dry vegetables in summer to eat in winter, and drink kahwa, a green tea with saffron, cardamom and almonds. On special days, a [[@kashmiri-wazwan|wazwan]] feast may include dozens of dishes, many slow-cooked with lamb. When spring finally returns, one of Asia's largest [[@oddity-tulip-mania|tulip gardens]] opens on the hills above the lake, and people come out to see the valley turn green again.

text: Mount Fuji is Japan's highest mountain, at 3,776 metres. It is a volcano with an almost perfectly even cone, often topped with snow. On a clear day it can be seen from Tokyo, about 100 km away.

It is special for more than its height. For centuries, Japanese people have treated Fuji as sacred, a place where gods live. Pilgrims have climbed it to pray. Poets have written about it and artists have painted it again and again. It appears on banknotes, stamps and countless souvenirs. For many people in Japan and abroad, its outline means "Japan".

st.reveal: Fuji's official climbing season runs from about early July to early September, when the trails are mostly free of snow and the mountain huts are open. Outside this time, the summit is icy, windy and dangerous.

myth: Mount Fuji is an extinct volcano that will never erupt again.
Fuji is classed as active. It has been quiet since 1707, but scientists watch it closely, and Japanese authorities have plans ready in case it erupts again.

sec.t:
Fuji sits where three of the Earth's [[plate|tectonic plates]] meet. Its present cone is fairly young in geological terms. It grew on top of older volcanoes over roughly the past 10,000 to 17,000 years, as layer after layer of [[lava|lava]] and ash piled up. A tall, steep cone built of layers like this is called a stratovolcano.

Fuji last erupted in 1707. The eruption didn't send lava pouring down the slopes. Instead it blasted out ash and cinders for about two weeks. Ash fell on Edo, the city that later became [[@tokyo|Tokyo]], about 100 km away. Fuji has been quiet since, but it is still an active [[@volcano|volcano]], and scientists monitor it for small earthquakes and changes in shape.

Fuji appears in Japanese poems that are well over a thousand years old. Later, short [[@haiku|haiku]] poets wrote about it too.

The most famous pictures of Fuji are by the artist Katsushika Hokusai. In the 1830s he made a series of woodblock prints called *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji*. One of them, *The Great Wave off Kanagawa*, shows a huge curling wave with tiny Fuji in the distance. It became one of the best-known images in the world and influenced European painters like Van Gogh and Monet.

About 200,000 people climb Fuji each summer, during the official season from about July to early September. There are four main trails, divided into ten stations. Most climbers take a bus to the fifth station, about halfway up, then walk the rest. The path is a zigzag of loose volcanic gravel, and the climb usually takes five to seven hours.

Many climb through the night, resting in mountain huts, to reach the summit for sunrise. The Japanese call this view *goraiko*. The air at the top has about a third less oxygen than at sea level, so climbers can get altitude sickness.

Crowds have become a problem. From 2025, the government charges climbers 4,000 yen each on the main trails, limits numbers and closes the gates to people who try to climb overnight without booking a hut.

From the north, Fuji is often reflected in five lakes at its base. In spring, cherry blossoms frame it. The bullet train between Tokyo and Osaka passes close by, and passengers rush to the right-hand windows when it comes into view. Fuji is often hidden by cloud, so a clear sight of it still feels like luck.

text: Bengali, or Bangla, is spoken as a first language by about 23 crore people, which places it among the ten most spoken languages on Earth. It is the national language of Bangladesh and an official language of West Bengal and Tripura in India. The 2011 Census found it was the second most spoken language in India after Hindi.

What makes it special is partly its size and partly its story. Bengali has a rich tradition of poems, songs and novels, a Nobel Prize-winning poet, and a day honoured by the whole world because people fought for the right to use it.

st.reveal: In 1952, what is now Bangladesh was part of Pakistan, whose leaders wanted Urdu as the only national language. Students in Dhaka protested for Bengali, and several were killed by police on 21 February. UNESCO chose that day in 1999 to honour every mother tongue.

Bengali is a separate language with its own script, grammar and over a thousand years of writing. It is a cousin of Hindi, since both grew from older Indian languages, but speakers of one cannot easily understand the other.

sec.t:
When British India was divided in 1947, East Bengal became part of Pakistan, which also included lands more than 1,500 km away to the west. Most people in East Bengal spoke Bengali, but Pakistan's leaders announced that Urdu alone would be the national language.

Students in Dhaka protested. On 21 February 1952, police opened fire on a march, and several students were killed. The Language Movement grew, and Bengali was eventually accepted as one of Pakistan's national languages in 1956. The struggle fed into the later movement that created the independent country of [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]] in 1971.

In 1999, UNESCO declared 21 February International Mother Language Day. It has been marked around the world since 2000, to protect all languages, big and small.

{{story:bangladesh}}

Bengali grew out of older spoken languages of eastern India, called Prakrits, which descend from the same ancient roots as Sanskrit. The oldest known Bengali writings are the *Charyapada*, Buddhist songs from roughly a thousand years ago. A scholar found them in the royal library of Nepal in 1907.

Bengali has its own [[script|script]], with letters that hang from a line along the top. A very similar script is used for Assamese. Like most [[@scripts-india|Indian scripts]], it is an [[abugida|abugida]], where each consonant carries a built-in vowel.

sec.h: Tagore, Ray and a flood of new ideas
sec.t:
In the 1800s, [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], then called Calcutta, was the capital of British India. It became a hotbed of printing presses, schools, debate and new writing, a time often called the [[@bengali-renaissance|Bengal Renaissance]].

Its most famous writer is [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]]. In 1913 he became the first Asian to win the Nobel Prize, for *Gitanjali*, a collection of poems he translated into English himself. He wrote over 2,000 songs. Two of them became national anthems: *Jana Gana Mana* for India and *Amar Shonar Bangla* for Bangladesh.

Bengali children grow up with the nonsense rhymes of [[@sukumar-ray|Sukumar Ray]] and the [[@detective-stories|detective stories]] of his son, the film-maker [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]]. Bengali novelists such as Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay were read across India in translation. Bankim wrote *Vande Mataram*, which became India's national song.

Bengali speakers often describe their language as *mishti*, sweet, and it is common to hear people say it is one of the sweetest-sounding languages. That is a matter of taste, not science. But Bengali does have a gentle sound: its words often end in soft vowels.

In 2024, the Government of India added Bengali to its list of classical languages. On 21 February each year, people gather in Dhaka at the Shaheed Minar, the Martyrs' Monument, barefoot and carrying flowers, and sing a song written for the students of 1952.

text: एमेंटल जैसी चीज़ के छेद [[bacteria|बैक्टीरिया]] बनाते हैं। जब चीज़ पककर तैयार हो रही होती है, तो प्रोपियोनिबैक्टीरियम नाम के बैक्टीरिया कच्ची चीज़ के एक पदार्थ को खाते हैं और [[carbon-dioxide|कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड]] गैस छोड़ते हैं। गैस छोटी-छोटी जेबों में जमा होती है। जैसे-जैसे और गैस बनती है, ये जेबें फूलकर गोल छेद बन जाती हैं।

चीज़ बनाने वाले इन छेदों को "आँखें" कहते हैं। एमेंटल के बड़े पहिए जैसे गोले में ये चेरी जितने छोटे से लेकर अख़रोट जितने बड़े तक हो सकते हैं। यही बैक्टीरिया चीज़ को उसका मीठा, मेवे जैसा स्वाद देने में भी मदद करते हैं।
ज़्यादातर चीज़ में छेद होते ही नहीं। चेडर ठसाठस भरी होती है, और पनीर तो बिलकुल अलग तरीक़े से बनता है।

myth: चूहों को चीज़ किसी भी और खाने से ज़्यादा पसंद है।

sec.t:
चीज़ की शुरुआत दूध से होती है। चीज़ बनाने वाला उसमें मददगार [[@microbes-friendly|सूक्ष्मजीव]] और रेनेट नाम का एक [[enzyme|एंज़ाइम]] डालता है, जो दूध को नरम छेने और पानी जैसे मट्ठे में बदल देता है। छेने को दबाकर एक बड़ा पहिया बनाया जाता है और नमकीन पानी में भिगोया जाता है।

एमेंटल के लिए इस पहिए को फिर कई हफ़्तों के लिए एक गर्म कमरे में रखा जाता है, जहाँ तापमान अक्सर 20°C से थोड़ा ऊपर होता है। यहीं छेद बनाने वाले बैक्टीरिया जागते हैं। वे लैक्टिक [[acid|अम्ल]] खाते हैं, जो पहले दूसरे बैक्टीरिया ने बनाया था, और उसे कुछ नए पदार्थों में बदल देते हैं, जिनमें कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड भी है।

यह एक तरह का [[@fermentation|ख़मीर उठना]] है, बदलावों का वही परिवार जो दूध को दही बनाता है। चीज़ की बाहरी परत काफ़ी हद तक हवा-बंद होती है, इसलिए गैस आसानी से निकल नहीं पाती। वह कमज़ोर जगहों पर जमा होकर बाहर की ओर धक्का देती है, और गोल छेद बन जाते हैं।

लंबे समय तक लोग मानते रहे कि गैस जहाँ कहीं जमा हो जाए, वहीं छेद बन जाता है। फिर स्विट्ज़रलैंड के चीज़ बनाने वालों ने कुछ अजीब देखा। पिछले कुछ दशकों में उनकी चीज़ में छेद कम से कम होते जा रहे थे।

2015 में स्विस सरकार के शोध केंद्र एग्रोस्कोप के वैज्ञानिकों ने जवाब ढूँढ निकाला। पहले गायों को गोशाला में हाथ से खुली बाल्टियों में दुहा जाता था, और सूखी घास के नन्हे तिनके दूध में गिर जाते थे। ये तिनके गैस को शुरुआत की जगह देते थे, जैसे हर छेद के लिए एक बीज।

आजकल की दूध दुहने वाली मशीनें बंद और चमचमाती साफ़ होती हैं। दूध में लगभग कोई घास न होने से गैस को शुरू होने की जगह ही नहीं मिली। जब शोधकर्ताओं ने दूध में फिर से घास की थोड़ी-सी धूल मिलाई, तो छेद लौट आए।

{{story:bubbles-round}}

एमेंटल मध्य [[@switzerland|स्विट्ज़रलैंड]] की एमे घाटी से आती है। इसके पहिए दुनिया की सबसे बड़ी चीज़ में गिने जाते हैं, अक्सर 75 से 120 किलो के, यानी एक बड़े आदमी जितने या उससे भी भारी। एक पहिया उठाने के लिए दो लोग या एक मशीन चाहिए।

छेदों का असर सिर्फ़ शक्ल पर नहीं पड़ता। बहुत ज़्यादा छेद, या ग़लत आकार के छेद, चीज़ को चटका सकते हैं। जिस चीज़ में छेद होने चाहिए पर बिलकुल न हों, उसे "अंधी" कहते हैं। एक स्विस जानकार पहिए को थपथपाकर और आवाज़ सुनकर मोटा अंदाज़ा लगा सकता है कि अंदर आँखें कैसी बन रही हैं, कुछ वैसे ही जैसे हम तरबूज़ ठोककर परखते हैं।

छेद वाली दूसरी चीज़ में नॉर्वे की यार्ल्सबर्ग और ग्रूयेर शामिल हैं, जिसमें बस कुछ छोटी-छोटी आँखें होती हैं।

भारतीय चीज़ ज़्यादातर लंबे समय तक पकाए बिना बनाई जाती है, इसलिए उसमें छेद नहीं बनते। [[@cheese-paneer|पनीर]] गर्म दूध को नींबू के रस या सिरके से फाड़कर और फिर मट्ठा निचोड़कर बनता है। यह महीनों में नहीं, घंटों में तैयार हो जाता है।

भारत में कुछ पुरानी, पकाई गई चीज़ भी हैं। [[@kolkata|कोलकाता]] के पास के एक क़स्बे की बैंडेल चीज़ सदियों पहले पुर्तगाली बसने वाले लाए थे। यह छोटी-छोटी गोल टिकियों में आती है, धुएँ वाली भी और सादी भी। जम्मू-कश्मीर में कलाड़ी नाम की एक खिंचने वाली चीज़ को तब तक तला जाता है जब तक वह बाहर से कुरकुरी और अंदर से लिसलिसी न हो जाए।

और सबसे अजीब बात? एमेंटल के अंदर के बुलबुले लगभग पूरी तरह गोल होते हैं, और इसकी वजह वही है जो साबुन के बुलबुलों के गोल होने की है। यह तुम [[@bubbles-round|बुलबुले गोल क्यों होते हैं]] में जान सकते हो।

text: A shop starts with what something costs it: the price it paid the supplier, plus rent, electricity, wages and transport. Then it adds a bit extra as profit. That is the basic price.

But the shop also watches what other shops charge, how many people want the item and how much it has in stock. If lots of people want something and there is little of it, the price goes up. If nobody is buying, the price drops. Shops also use small tricks, like ending prices in 99, to make things feel cheaper. In India, the law adds one more rule: never above the MRP.

st.prompt: Why do so many shops price things at ₹99 or $9.99 instead of ₹100 or $10?

options.t: The price feels much cheaper because the first digit is smaller
It saves the shop money on coins
The law says prices must end in 9

st.reveal: People read numbers from left to right and pay most attention to the first digit. So ₹99 feels closer to ₹90 than to ₹100, even though it is only one rupee less. Researchers call this the left-digit effect.

sec.t:
Prices shift when supply or demand changes. In 2023, heavy rains and heat damaged tomato crops in parts of India, and in some cities [[@tomatoes|tomatoes]] crossed ₹200 a kilo for a while. Families switched to other recipes until the new harvest arrived.

In the United States, the price of eggs jumped in 2022 and 2023 when bird flu killed millions of hens. When supply fell, people competed for fewer eggs, and the price rose. When supply recovered, prices came down again.

In India, every packaged product must show an MRP, or maximum retail price, which includes all taxes. Shops may sell for less, but not more. This rule protects shoppers in places where they cannot easily compare prices.

In the United States, there is no MRP. Price tags usually leave out sales tax, which is added at the till and varies from state to state. Visitors from India are often surprised when a $10 shirt costs more than $10 at the counter. [[@taxes|Taxes]] are part of every price, whether you see them or not.

In many Indian markets, from Sarojini Nagar in [[@delhi|Delhi]] to small weekly haats, bargaining is normal. The seller starts high, the buyer offers low, and they meet somewhere in the middle. Supermarkets and big stores usually have fixed prices printed on labels.

Fixed price tags only became common in the late 1800s, when big department stores in cities like New York and Paris wanted to serve many customers quickly. Before that, haggling was common almost everywhere.

sec.h: Prices that change by the minute
sec.t:
Some prices change constantly. Airline tickets, hotel rooms and taxi apps use [[@coding-maths|computer programs]] that raise prices when demand is high and lower them when it is quiet. A cab ride in Mumbai during a downpour may cost much more than the same ride on a dry afternoon.

Shops also use "loss leaders": they sell a few popular items very cheaply, even at a loss, to bring people in, hoping they will buy other things too.

Understanding prices helps you spot a real bargain. Check the price per kilo or per litre, not just the price on the packet, and remember that a "buy one get one free" deal only helps if you need two. Paying by phone with [[@upi-payments|UPI]] or by card makes spending easy, which is one reason it helps to stop and do the maths first.
